summary: On a deep-space mission, a solar storm can flood a crew with radiation, and no clinic is within reach. MissionVitals is a mission-control-style dashboard that watches an astronaut’s radiation exposure, heart rate, blood markers, reaction time and mood together, and sets one clear status: Nominal, Caution or Warning. In our seven-day demo, a solar flare hits on Day 3. Radiation spikes, a Warning fires, and a WhatsApp alert reaches the ground team. The next morning, rising inflammation is flagged as likely radiation-related because the spike came first, and Gemini explains what it means and what to do. Each astronaut is compared to their own first three days, with simulated blood values anchored in NASA’s data, and fixed rules, not AI, trigger every alarm. This answers the challenge by turning scattered measurements into early, plain-language guidance when lab access is limited. As crews travel farther from Earth, tools like this could help them spot problems sooner and act with confidence. Demo readings are simulated and labeled as such.
details: Far from Earth, an astronaut can’t just visit a clinic, so we built MissionVitals, a dashboard that helps catch health problems early. It watches radiation, heart rate, blood markers (inflammation, a stress hormone, and blood sugar), reaction time, and mood, and compares each reading to that astronaut’s own first three days instead of a generic average. Then it gives one clear status: Nominal, Caution, or Warning. Simple built-in rules set every alarm, so a warning never waits on AI. Google’s Gemini steps in afterward to explain what’s happening in plain language and suggest what to do next. In our simulated seven-day mission, a solar flare on Day 3 triggers a Warning and a WhatsApp alert to the ground team. The next morning, a blood test shows rising inflammation, and because a radiation spike came first, the app flags it as likely radiation-related and not just a bug going around. Every Warning prompts the astronaut to contact the flight surgeon, and nothing in the app diagnoses anyone. We see it as a prototype for the software that future onboard blood testing could feed. Daily check-ins (mood, sleep, stress, and a short memory test) are saved, and the astronaut can ask a chatbox questions about their own entries. We built it with Python, Streamlit, the Gemini API, a Cloudflare Worker, and Twilio’s WhatsApp sandbox, and we used Claude as a coding assistant. The mission data in the demo is simulated and clearly labeled, and nothing in the app diagnoses anyone. What makes it different is that it connects cause and effect instead of just displaying numbers, and keeps AI out of the alarm itself. We designed it to be safe, reliable, and easy to understand for someone under stress.
